title: Marriage (Mark 10:1–12)
hook: asked about divorce, he points back to creation; churches today apply this in differing ways

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was salt; your line, salt, and peace. Now a new stretch of Mark: the road to Jerusalem.

Chapter ten, and the road turns south. Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea and the land beyond the Jordan, and crowds gather again. Some Pharisees come with a question, and Mark tells us it's a test. Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife? The Law of Moses allowed a man to write his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away, and teachers disagreed sharply over what reasons were good enough. Whatever Jesus says, someone will be unhappy. Almost everyone listening knows a marriage that held, and one that broke. He goes not to the rules, but back to the beginning.
screen: `THE ROAD TURNS SOUTH.` → `IS IT LAWFUL?` → `BACK TO THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: What did Moses command, he asks. Moses allowed a certificate of divorce, they say. Jesus says Moses wrote that because of the hardness of your hearts. It's a different Greek word from the hard hearts in the boat on day one ninety-one, but the same picture: a heart gone stiff. Then he reaches past Moses to Genesis: from the beginning God made them male and female, and a man shall leave his father and mother, and the two shall be one flesh. Then the line still heard at weddings, in the King James Bible: "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." Asunder means apart. Later, in the house, he goes further with the disciples: whoever divorces and marries another commits adultery. Mark also includes a wife divorcing her husband, which fit Roman law more than the Jewish custom of the day. And divorce then often meant a woman sent away with a piece of paper, and often nothing to live on. Many readers hear in his words a protection for the one most likely to be discarded. Churches apply this differently, and each takes it seriously. The Catholic Church teaches that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, and it can declare that a marriage was never valid, an annulment. Orthodox churches hold marriage as lifelong, yet may allow a second marriage with a service of repentance. Many Protestant churches allow divorce in some circumstances, such as adultery or abandonment, reading this alongside Matthew and Paul. What they share is the starting point Jesus chose: not the loophole, but the beginning.
screen: `WHAT DID MOSES COMMAND?` · `FOR THE HARDNESS OF YOUR HEART.` · `FROM THE BEGINNING: ONE FLESH.` · `CHURCHES APPLY IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `WHAT THEREFORE GOD HATH JOINED TOGETHER, LET NOT MAN PUT ASUNDER.`

segments.voice: Hold one marriage in your mind: your own, your parents', a friend's, a couple just starting, one that's struggling right now, or even one that ended, and the people still living with that. Picture them both kindly: what do they need? Patience, time together, rest. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, wish them well, slowly and on purpose.
Marriage. Asked about divorce, Jesus answers with the beginning: two becoming one flesh, joined by God.
Your line: what god joined. Day two hundred, and still walking together.

howItsDone: Many Christian wedding services echo Mark 10:9, that what God has joined no one should put asunder, and many churches pray for married couples during worship; churches differ on divorce and remarriage, from the Catholic Church's annulment process to the Orthodox and many Protestant churches' provisions for remarriage.

Sensitive day. Three church positions summarized: Catholic (indissolubility of a valid sacramental marriage; declarations of nullity), Orthodox (lifelong ideal; second marriage permitted with a penitential rite, within limits), many Protestant (divorce allowed in some circumstances, e.g. adultery per Matthew 19:9, abandonment per 1 Corinthians 7:15).
